extracted.intended_audience: clinicians and researchers invited to peer review manuscripts for The BMJ
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for clinicians and researchers who are asked to peer review manuscripts for The BMJ, covering how to become a reviewer, procedural obligations (confidentiality, conflicts), and detailed criteria for assessing research and other article types.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open peer review and reviewer identification
rubrics_metrics.description: The BMJ has fully open peer review for all articles which means the names of reviewers are disclosed to the author of the paper. We ask reviewers to sign their reports and declare any competing interests on any manuscripts we send them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accepted research and analysis papers will usually have their prepublication history posted alongside them (reviewers’ comments, author responses, protocols etc.). Reviewers should be aware their names may be disclosed to authors and (for accepted papers) comments may be posted with the paper; reviewers must sign reports and declare competing interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidentiality of manuscripts
rubrics_metrics.description: An author’s manuscript must remain confidential until it is published, and you must not disclose any information about an unpublished manuscript, including your review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You may refer to the journal which requested your review and the fact you have reviewed an article for it, but you may not post details of the article reviewed or any part of the review that would breach confidentiality. Do not contact authors directly; direct queries through the editorial office.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ownership and licensing of reviews
rubrics_metrics.description: You will remain the owner of the review you submit to us. In submitting your review to The BMJ you are agreeing to licence your work to us so that we may use it for the purposes outlined below. If published, your review will be published under the same license as the article.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the manuscript is transferred to another BMJ journal, your review may be passed on and could be published (you will be contacted for permission). Ensure you have consent from any co-reviewer or third party who contributed before submitting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of reviewers vs editors
rubrics_metrics.description: As a reviewer you will be advising the editors, who make the final decision (aided by an editorial committee for all research articles and most analysis articles).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide clear, evidence-based advice to support editorial decision-making. Reviewers will be informed of decisions by email; if the article is not accepted the editors will still pass on reviewer comments to the authors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accepting invitations and timeliness
rubrics_metrics.description: If you feel qualified to judge a particular manuscript, you should agree to review only if you are able to return a review within the proposed or mutually agreed time-frame.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you cannot review, decline promptly and, if possible, suggest alternative reviewers based on expertise and without personal considerations or intent to influence outcome.

rubrics_metrics.name: Declaring competing interests (conflicts of interest)
rubrics_metrics.description: During the review process we ask you to declare any potentially conflicting or competing interests (which could be personal, financial, intellectual, professional, political or religious in nature) so that editors can assess these and factor them into their decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The BMJ restricts requests to financial interests to increase disclosure. Before submitting, reviewers are asked specific questions (eg reimbursement for attending a symposium; fees for speaking, consulting, organising education; research funds; employment in past five years by an organisation that may gain/lose financially; stocks or shares). If you have any competing interests please declare them. Refer major concerns to the editorial office before beginning review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer conduct: fairness, honesty, and professionalism
rubrics_metrics.description: As a reviewer you must provide a fair, honest, and unbiased assessment of the strengths and weaknesses of the manuscript.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be specific in your critique and provide supporting evidence with appropriate references. Be professional and refrain from being hostile, inflammatory, libellous, or derogatory. Make constructive suggestions rather than personal attacks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be specific and evidence-based (do not overgeneralise)
rubrics_metrics.description: Be specific in your critique, and provide supporting evidence with appropriate references to substantiate general statements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If work is unclear because of missing analyses, explain what additional analyses would clarify the work. Do not ask reviewers to extend the work beyond its current scope — recommend feasible clarifications or analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not use peer review to gain sight of work without intent to review
rubrics_metrics.description: You should not agree to review a manuscript just to gain sight of it with no intention of submitting a review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you accept, follow through and complete the review. If unable to do so, decline promptly and suggest alternatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Co-reviewer use, consent and disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: It is your responsibility to ensure that you obtain the consent of any co-reviewer or other third party who may have contributed to your review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When submitting your review disclose the identity of any co-reviewer and any potential conflicting or competing interests they may have.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidential handling and disposal of manuscript copies
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers should not retain the manuscript for personal use and should destroy copies after submitting their review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you discuss the manuscript with a professional colleague whose input you request, ensure they are aware of the confidential nature of the discussion and must not disclose information until publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporting suspected misconduct or duplicate publication
rubrics_metrics.description: If you have concerns that misconduct occurred during either the research or the writing and submission of the manuscript, or you notice substantial similarity between the manuscript and a concurrent submission to another journal or a published article; please let the journal editor know.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flag suspected fraud, plagiarism, duplicate submission, or ethical problems to the editorial office rather than addressing them in the review comments alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of reporting checklists and trial protocols
rubrics_metrics.description: Checklists for reporting statements such as CONSORT, PRISMA, and STROBE (and the protocol for an RCT) should be checked: Do these properly match what is in the manuscript?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify that supplemental checklists and the study protocol correspond to the manuscript and do not reveal information that should be better reported in the manuscript or that raise questions about the work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess overall importance and relevance
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers should consider for all articles: Is the article important? Will it help our readers to make better decisions and, if so, how? Will the article add enough to existing knowledge? Does the article read well and make sense? Does it have a clear message?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comment on the article's potential impact on clinicians, researchers, policymakers, educators, or patients and whether a general medical journal is the right place for it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality (research articles)
rubrics_metrics.description: Originality - does the work add enough to what is already in the published literature? If so, what does it add?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite relevant references to support your comments on originality and identify what is novel about the contribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Importance to general readers (research articles)
rubrics_metrics.description: Importance of the work to general readers - does this work matter to clinicians, researchers, policymakers, educators, or patients? Will it help our readers to make better decisions and, if so, how? Is a general medical journal the right place for it?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the breadth and practical implications of the findings for The BMJ's readership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity of research question and whether it is answered
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the research question clearly defined and appropriately answered?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether study objectives/hypotheses are explicit and whether the analyses and results address them convincingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overall study design adequacy
rubrics_metrics.description: Overall design of study - appropriate and adequate to answer the research question?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge suitability of study design, control/comparison groups, randomisation, blinding, sample size justification, and other design features relative to the question.

rubrics_metrics.name: Participants: description and representativeness
rubrics_metrics.description: Participants - adequately described, their conditions defined, inclusion and exclusion criteria described? How representative were the authors of patients whom this evidence might affect?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check whether participant selection, recruitment, and baseline characteristics are reported clearly and whether external validity/generalizability is addressed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods: completeness, outcomes and ethics
rubrics_metrics.description: Methods - adequately described? Main outcome measure clear? Is the study fully reported in line with the appropriate reporting statement or checklist? Was the study ethical (this may go beyond simply whether the study was approved by an ethics committee or IRB)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure sufficient methodological detail to reproduce/assess the study. Confirm the primary outcome is defined and appropriate, and evaluate ethical considerations including consent and approvals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Results: credibility and presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Results - answer the research question? Credible? Well presented?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether results are reported transparently (including negative findings), with appropriate statistics, confidence intervals, and tables/figures, and whether they support the conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation and conclusions justified by data
rubrics_metrics.description: Interpretation and conclusions - warranted by and sufficiently derived from/focused on the data? Discussed in the light of previous evidence? Is the message clear?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check that authors do not overstate implications, appropriately acknowledge limitations, and place findings in context of existing literature.

rubrics_metrics.name: References: currency and completeness
rubrics_metrics.description: References - up to date and relevant? Any glaring omissions?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify missing key citations or undue reliance on weak sources. Recommend relevant literature if appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstract, summary and key messages accuracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Abstract/summary/key messages/what this paper adds - reflect accurately what the paper says?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify that summaries mirror the main text and do not overclaim; ensure key messages are evidence-based and consistent with results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency between manuscript and supplemental files
rubrics_metrics.description: Documents in the supplemental files, eg. checklists for reporting statements such as CONSORT, PRISMA, and STROBE; and the protocol for an RCT. Do these properly match what is in the manuscript? Do they contain information that should be better reported in the manuscript, or raise questions about the work?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cross-check supplemental materials against the manuscript for discrepancies, omissions, or additions that affect interpretation or reporting quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patient and public reviewer perspective
rubrics_metrics.description: In addition to peer review, The BMJ also asks patient reviewers for their opinion on the importance and relevance of selected manuscripts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognise that patient/public reviewers focus on relevance, clarity, and patient-centred implications; see BMJ’s patient reviewer guidance/training materials for specifics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Becoming a reviewer: registration and declaring expertise
rubrics_metrics.description: If you would like to volunteer, please register for an account at our online editorial office to be added to our reviewer database. Fill in details such as keywords and special interests to show up in our reviewer database searches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include appropriate keywords and special interests (eg 'student' for BMJ Student) to improve matching with manuscripts. BMJ invites medical students to review for BMJ Student.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suggesting alternative reviewers ethically
rubrics_metrics.description: If you cannot review the manuscript and would like to suggest an alternative reviewer, please reply to the invitation email to let us know.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When recommending alternatives base suggestions on expertise and avoid personal considerations or any intention that the manuscript receive a specific outcome.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial transparency: provenance statements
rubrics_metrics.description: At the end of every accepted editorial, research article, clinical review, practice article, analysis article, feature, and head-to-head article The BMJ will add a statement explaining the article's provenance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provenance options include combinations of 'commissioned' or 'not commissioned' and 'externally peer reviewed' or 'not externally peer reviewed'; reviewers should be aware their role contributes to this provenance statement.
